subject: Anatomy
summary: The rectum is the final 12‑15 cm of the large intestine, storing feces before evacuation. Its anatomy determines the presentation of bleeding, pain, and obstruction.

sections.p: The rectum continues the sigmoid colon and ends at the anorectal junction, where the internal anal sphincter begins.
b: Length ≈ 12‑15 cm
Divided into three zones: upper, middle, lower

sections.p: It lies in the pelvis, anterior to the sacrum and coccyx, posterior to the prostate/uterus, and is covered by the mesorectum.
b: Mucosa: columnar epithelium with goblet cells
Submucosa contains hemorrhoidal vascular plexus
Muscularis: inner circular, outer longitudinal

sections.p: Anteriorly it contacts the bladder (men) or uterus (women); laterally the levator ani and piriformis; posteriorly the sacrum and coccyx.
b: Important for surgical planes
Tumor spread follows these fascial planes

sections.p: Arterial supply comes from the superior rectal artery (branch of IMA) and the middle/lower rectal arteries (branches of internal iliac). Venous drainage mirrors arteries to portal and systemic systems.
b: Superior rectal → portal system (risk of portal hypertension varices)
Middle/lower rectal → systemic (risk of hemorrhoids)

sections.p: Parasympathetic innervation via pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2‑S4) stimulates motility; sympathetic fibers (L1‑L2) control sphincter tone. Sensory afferents convey pain from the upper two‑thirds (visceral) and lower third (somatic).
b: Visceral pain is vague, referred to lower back
Somatic pain is sharp, perianal

sections.p: Stores feces, coordinates defecation via reflexes (gastrocolic, recto‑anal), and maintains continence through internal/external sphincters.
b: Recto‑anal inhibitory reflex relaxes internal sphincter when rectum distends
External sphincter under voluntary control

sections.p: Rectal pathology often presents with bleeding, pain, or altered bowel habits. Understanding anatomy guides examination, imaging, and surgery.
b: Rectal cancer: arises from mucosa, spreads along mesorectal fascia
Hemorrhoids: dilation of superior/inferior rectal plexus
Fistula-in-ano: tracks through intersphincteric space
Trauma: can perforate posterior wall against sacrum

t.b: Detects masses, tone, fissures; a firm, irregular mass suggests cancer
Visualizes mucosa; ulcerative colitis shows continuous erythema from rectum
Staging rectal cancer; assesses mesorectal involvement, sphincter invasion

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Rectal bleeding without upper GI signs points to colorectal source.
An empty rectum with a gush of stool on withdrawal suggests Hirschsprung disease in infants.
Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum is characteristic of ulcerative colitis.

whenToSeekHelp: Profuse rectal bleeding causing hemodynamic instability
Sudden severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs (possible perforation)
Unexplained weight loss with persistent change in bowel habit

faq.q: Why is rectal bleeding often painless in ulcerative colitis?
faq.a: Inflammation is limited to the mucosa, sparing deeper pain fibers.

faq.q: What distinguishes a hemorrhoid from a rectal tumor on exam?
faq.a: Hemorrhoids are compressible vascular cushions; tumors are firm, fixed, and may ulcerate.

faq.q: When is a colonoscopy preferred over sigmoidoscopy?
faq.a: When the disease may extend beyond the rectosigmoid or when full colonic assessment is needed.

exam: Describe the arterial supply of the rectum and its clinical relevance.
Explain how the recto‑anal inhibitory reflex contributes to continence.
Outline the staging criteria for rectal cancer on MRI.
